language.label: Language
explain.nakedSingle: {cell} has only candidate {digit} left; every other digit is eliminated by a peer. Therefore {cell} = {digit}.
explain.hiddenSingle: In {unit}, digit {digit} can only be placed in {cell}. Therefore {cell} = {digit}.
explain.lockedCandidatesPointing: Inside {box}, digit {digit} is confined to {line} ({spots}). Therefore {digit} can be removed from the rest of {line}: {eliminations}.
explain.lockedCandidatesClaiming: In {line}, digit {digit} is confined to {box} ({spots}). Therefore {digit} can be removed from the other cells of {box}: {eliminations}.
explain.nakedPair: In {unit}, {cells} contain only candidates {digits}, forming a naked pair. Those two digits must occupy these two cells, so remove them elsewhere in the unit: {eliminations}.
explain.hiddenPair: In {unit}, both digits {digits} can appear only in {cells}. This hidden pair locks the two cells, so other candidates can be removed: {eliminations}.
explain.nakedTriple: In {unit}, {cells} collectively use only {digits}, forming a naked triple. Those digits must occupy these three cells, so eliminate them elsewhere in the unit: {eliminations}.
explain.hiddenTriple: In {unit}, digits {digits} can only appear in {cells}, forming a hidden triple. Those cells are locked to these digits, so remove their other candidates: {eliminations}.
explain.xWing: Digit {digit} has exactly two positions in each of the {baseUnits}, and they cover only the {coverUnits}. This is an X-Wing. Each cover line needs one {digit}, so remove it from the rest: {eliminations}.
explain.swordfish: Digit {digit} appears in only 2-3 positions in each of the {baseUnits}, covering only the {coverUnits} in total. This is a Swordfish: the three copies of {digit} must occupy those three cover lines, so remove {digit} from the rest of them: {eliminations}.
explain.jellyfish: Digit {digit} is restricted to only 2-4 positions in each of the {baseUnits}, covering exactly the {coverUnits}. This is a Jellyfish. Those four cover lines must hold all four copies of {digit}, so eliminate it from elsewhere: {eliminations}.
explain.yWing: Pivot {pivot} has candidates {pivotDigits}. The two wings {wing1}({wing1Digits}) and {wing2}({wing2Digits}) both see the pivot and share digit {digit}. Whichever value the pivot takes, at least one wing must be {digit}, so cells seeing both wings cannot be {digit}: {eliminations}.
explain.xyzWing: Pivot {pivot} has three candidates {pivotDigits}. Wings {wing1}({wing1Digits}) and {wing2}({wing2Digits}) both see the pivot and share {digit}. Whichever candidate the pivot takes, one of the pivot or wings must be {digit}, so any cell seeing all three cannot be {digit}: {eliminations}.
explain.skyscraper: Digit {digit} has exactly two candidates in each of the {baseUnits}, sharing {baseUnit} as a base. This forms a Skyscraper. At least one roof ({roofs}) must be {digit}, so cells that see both roofs cannot be {digit}: {eliminations}.
explain.twoStringKite: Digit {digit} has exactly two positions in {rowUnit} and in {colUnit}. {boxEndpoints} share a box. If a cell seeing both free ends {freeEnds} were {digit}, both free ends would be false, forcing both box endpoints to be {digit} in the same box, a contradiction. Therefore such a cell cannot be {digit}: {eliminations}.
explain.uniqueRectangle: The four cells {corners} span two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes. Three of them are restricted to {pair}, while {extraCell} also has {extraDigits}. If {extraCell} were {pair}, the four corners could swap values and yield a second solution. Under the uniqueness assumption, remove {eliminations}.
explain.simpleColouring.sameColour: For digit {digit}, two same-coloured candidates ({conflictCells}) of colour {colour} see each other. Both cannot be true, so the whole colour is impossible. Eliminate {eliminations}.
explain.simpleColouring.bothColours: Build a colour chain for digit {digit}: exactly one of colours A and B must be true. {eliminations} sees candidates of both colours, so it cannot be {digit} whichever colour is true. It is therefore eliminated.
explain.wWing: Endpoints {endpoints} are both bivalue cells {digits} and do not see each other directly. Digit {linkDigit} has only two positions in {strongUnit}, {linkCells} (a strong link), each seeing one endpoint. If an endpoint is not {eliminated} (so it is {linkDigit}), the strong-link cell it sees cannot be {linkDigit}; the strong link then forces the other link cell to {linkDigit}, which forces the other endpoint to be {eliminated}. Hence at least one endpoint is {eliminated}. Therefore cells seeing both endpoints cannot be {eliminated}: {eliminations}.
explain.xyChain: Starting at {start}, truth propagates through the bivalue chain {chain}. If the start is not {digit}, the final cell {end} must be {digit}, and vice versa. At least one endpoint is {digit}, so cells seeing both endpoints cannot be {digit}: {eliminations}.
ocr.title: Scan or photograph a puzzle
ocr.desc: Use the camera or choose a photo. The image is processed only on this device.
ocr.guide.align: Fill the frame with the 9×9 grid and keep it straight.
ocr.guide.light: Use even light and avoid shadows or glare.
ocr.guide.focus: Hold steady and keep every digit sharp.
ocr.offline: Offline recognition; the image is never uploaded.
ocr.failed.noGrid: No 9×9 grid found. Fill the frame with the grid and try again.
ocr.failed.unclear: The image is too unclear. Improve the light and hold the camera steady.
ocr.failed.invalid: The recognised digits break Sudoku rules. Check the image and try again.
ocr.failed.unsolvable: The recognised puzzle has no solution. Check the image.
ocr.failed.engine: The offline OCR engine could not start. You can still import an 81-character string.
ocr.failed.noCamera: The camera is unavailable. Choose a photo instead.
ocr.successVerify: Recognition complete. Please check the board.
